#1243. Celtic's European opponents are plankton in football's great ocean... but Portuguese second-tier strugglers Torreense have already made waves in Europe this season

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 12:29 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 12:33 EST, 25 November 2026

Even for aficionados of the continental game, the draw for the Europa League this year was likely to cause a degree of puzzlement.

While not the only outfit to be making its debut in one of UEFA’s competitions, the name of S.C.U. Torreense rang precious few bells among supporters of clubs with a vested interest in how the cards might fall. And little wonder.

The Portuguese side are plankton in football’s great ocean. Not only have they never played on this stage before, they haven’t even come close to it.

An extraordinary triumph in the Portuguese Cup final – the Taca de Portugal – against Sporting Lisbon in May was their ticket to this journey. In all likelihood, this European adventure will be their first and their last.

It is, of course, not the done thing for anyone connected with any particular club to express a preference as to who they might be drawn against. But representatives of any one of the 35 other sides present at the Grimaldi Forum in Monaco in late August who claimed they weren’t privately hoping for a match against the men from the small city of Torres Vedras were lying.

Never mind Benfica, Porto and Sporting Lisbon, the traditional footballing powerhouses of that nation. In terms of support, stature and history, this outfit are a world removed from the likes of Braga and Vitoria Guimaraes, the perennial challengers to the big three.

Torreense players celebrate their victory over Armenian side Ararat in their last European tie

Torreense’s place in the food chain is underscored by the fact that they can’t even play European matches in their 2,400-capacity Estadio Manuel Marques home because it doesn’t match UEFA criteria.

For the purposes of the Europa League, their fans, who primarily hail from a place which sits 25 miles north of Lisbon, will have to travel to Leiria, which is 60 miles north of their home.

Those looking to pick up a late ticket for the visit of Celtic should have no concerns. Built for Euro 2004, the Estadio Municipal de Leiria holds 23,888 spectators. Torreense, who were a tier three side as recently as 2022, draw an average crowd of around 1,300.

The fact is that it’s not only a second division Portuguese side which Martin O’Neill’s men will face on matchday five. It’s a struggling one.

After ten matches in Liga Portugal 2, Joao Nuno’s men lie 13th of 18, 31st place overall in Portugal. They’ve won just twice this season, against Amarante and Benfica B, and have already had their cup defence ended by Benfica’s big boys.

Nuno was only appointed at the end of October after Luis Tralhao, who lifted the only major honour in the club’s history, was fired after a dismal start.

Portuguese coach Joao Nuno only took charge at the struggling second-tier side this season

Yet the concern for O’Neill and his players is that the Torreense which routinely fails to impress in its domestic division bears little resemblance to the one which has so far pitched up on its maiden European adventure.

In one of the most eye-catching results of the opening night, the Portuguese minnows travelled to Norway and defeated Lillestrom, a respected name throughout Europe, 2-1.

Sunderland were the first visitors to Leiria in October. What a game Torreense gave the Premier League side, leading by a goal only to narrowly lose the match late on.

While a 4-1 loss to Celtic’s old foes Ferencvaros in Budapest was something of a reality check, Nuno’s players fought back from a goal down to beat Ararat-Armenia in injury time last time out at their adopted home.

So, despite being wretched in their own league, they have six points in the Europa League and presently sit in 19th place, above the likes of Real Sociedad, AC Milan and Marseille.

With nine points possibly being enough to squeeze through to the play-off round, a famous win against Celtic could do the trick with three games to spare. With around £400,000 earned in prize money for any victory, you’d better believe they’ll be up for this.

Having just about lived to tell the tale last month, Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris gave Celtic a warning about what lies in store on Thursday.

Despite their lowly status, Torreense are above AC Milan, Celtic and Marseille in the table

‘It’s a good team they know how to manage this kind of game,’ said the Frenchman. ‘They’re well organised and hard to break down with this deep block. They try to seize every opportunity.’

A limited side which sits in and plays with caution? Those Celtic supporters who had the misfortune to watch their favourites fail to break down an atrocious Kairat Almaty outfit across 210 minutes little over a year ago will be rightly concerned.

While the Parkhead men’s poor record on the road across many years includes some thumpings at the hands of super clubs including Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain, there have been enough stumbles against lesser sides to ensure nothing can be taken for granted.

O’Neill will point to the displays in last season’s victories away to Feyenoord and Stuttgart as examples of what he’s looking for. While not on his watch, the catastrophe away to Kairat remains a useful illustration of what may happen if the players aren’t at it.

With an early goal likely to kick the legs from under Torreense, Celtic cannot allow them to feel comfortable in their shape.

In order to disrupt the Portuguese, it will be a night for the visitors to play with speed and imagination. To get in behind their defence, O’Neill’s wingers need to shine.

Sunderland required a late goal from Noah Sadiki to emerge with a victory on their trip to Leiria

This will have informed the veteran’s thinking as he sought to draft in a replacement for the injured Mika Baur.

While bringing in Joel van den Berg would have made sense from a positional point of view, Jota has started to show signs that he’s moving through the levels after a year-and-a-half out injured. A goal or an assist on his return to his homeland would allow the former Benfica man to underscore that point.

A constant threat against St Mirren, Yang Hyun-jun should start on the right flank ahead of Haissem Hassan. Together with Seb Tounekti, the Egyptian increasingly feels like a peripheral player.

Even if Benjamin Nygren is available again after a heel injury, O’Neill will be loath to drop Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain or Luke McCowan after both showed up well when played alongside Callum McGregor in the weekend win.

The issue of Kasper Hogh’s 16-game goal drought will only become pertinent if the free-scoring Camilo Duran can first help to put the game to bed.

Fit-again winger Jota could feature for Celtic on his return to Portuguese soil

Celtic badly need this to be a rare straightforward evening on the road in Europe. Goodness knows, they’ve had precious few of those in recent times.

A win to go with the one they claimed last time out against Besiktas would leave them in a decent position in the competition, with a further four points from their remaining matches with Omonia, Marseille and Union Saint-Gilloise then assuring them of progression.

Anything other than that outcome tonight doesn’t bear thinking about. Almost 60 years on from Jock Stein’s side becoming sporting immortals by defeating Inter Milan in Lisbon, their successors must tick a box and ensure tiny Torreense’s reputation in the game remains as lowly as it has ever been.

#1242. Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and said: “You held it together. You got through it.” It showed how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

Kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

Bayern Munich and England's Ballon d'Or winner doing what he does best 🎯 https://t.co/yWNburqkpg

For his club, that is 19 goals more than any other player in the top five European leagues. And the most since Cristiano Ronaldo scored 61 for Real Madrid in 2014-15. Kane won last season’s Golden Shoe by nine goals from Erling Haaland. He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Neither Kylian Mbappé nor Lamine Yamal, his closest rivals, scored in any finals.

Both gave interviews declaring why they should win the Ballon d’Or. Kane? “I don’t like talking about myself,” he said. “The 73 goals speak for themselves.” They do.

Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. Take his two goals against the Democratic Republic of Congo at the World Cup that saved his team and Thomas Tuchel from an embarrassing early exit.

The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

“A brilliant captain, a remarkable player and someone who has given football fans across the world so many unforgettable moments,” Prince William wrote on Instagram.

Kane, the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to win the award, is also the ultimate team player – so fulfilling that “collective performance” criteria – and a captain who leads by example on and off the pitch. Fair play? He was last booked in January and was cautioned just three times in 68 games and not at all in any of his 13 appearances this season.

And he works hard, so very hard. Kane was in the top 10 for total distance covered at the World Cup, despite playing a game fewer than most of the others on the list. And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

That work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and said he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

They probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

For the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more important than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

There's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN

Hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

First up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has announced Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

In total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

#1241. Inside Raheem Sterling's rise from childhood tragedy and poverty to England superstar at the peak of his powers - but Lamborghini crash and laughing gas addiction leave him staring into the abyss

Published: 08:02 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 13:10 EST, 25 November 2026

In September, shortly after pleading guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession, Raheem Sterling shared a statement on social media.

The goal, he implied with a picture of graffiti on a wall, was to 'be better than yesterday' and the intention was to seek 'progress over perfection', as he captioned the image.

But for the former England and Manchester City star to move forward, he has had to fall a long way.

The 31-year-old avoided prison, but was handed a 12-month suspended sentence and 100 hours of community service at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court after he was involved in a dangerous crash in May. Sterling had been driving his £270,000 Lamborghini Urus SUV while under the influence of laughing gas, with multiple motorists spotting him using balloons at the wheel while careening down the M25 and M3 motorways.

During his sentencing hearing, Sterling revealed that he has undergone a 12-day stint in rehab soon after the arrest, after contacting UK addiction services.

The number of footballers in history who have found themselves entangled with the British justice system is not a small one. But against the backdrop of Sterling's personal story, his fall is a particularly poignant one. The former international built a remarkable career out of a difficult upbringing.

Raheem Sterling has been handed a suspended sentence and 100 hours of community service after being convicted of dangerous driving

The former Manchester City star has experienced some of the highest heights in professional football - but now languishes without a club

Sterling lost his father at the age of just two to gun violence, prompting his mother's move from his birthplace of Kingston, Jamaica to the London suburb of Neasden.

Speaking to the Players' Tribune in 2018, Sterling admitted that the tragedy had 'shaped his entire life'.

'For a few years, we lived with our grandmother in Kingston, and I remember watching the other kids with their mums and just feeling really jealous,' he revealed. 'I didn't fully understand what my mum was doing for us. I just knew that she was gone. My grandma was amazing, but everybody wants their mum at that age.'

His father's shocking death also inspired a gun tattoo inked on his leg above his right 'shooting' foot, there as part of a promise he had made that he 'would never touch a gun in his lifetime'. Although the tattoo prompted criticism from anti-gun campaigners in 2018, Sterling was adamant that his message was aligned with theirs, with the player backed by the FA.

After moving to England, his mother Nadine found work as a cleaner. Sterling and his siblings would sometimes help her during her early morning shifts cleaning hotels at 5am before their school day started. With rent a continual challenge for the family as money was tight, they moved house often.

But Sterling's prodigious talent on the football pitch was breaking through, with the winger asked to join Queens Park Rangers' youth set-up at just 10 years old.

Sacrifices were made to allow for this: in 2021, Sterling released a custom football boot with New Balance paying tribute to the three buses - the 18, the 182 and 140 - he had to catch to make the return journey from home near Wembley to the west London training ground, accompanied by his older sister Lakima.

'The red double-deckers with the blue wool '80s vibe on the seats,' he reminisced. 'Spent ages on those. We'd leave at 3.15 and get home at 11 pm. Every. Single. Day.

'She'd sit upstairs in the little cafe and chill until I was done with training. Imagine being 17 years old and doing that for your little brother. And I never once heard her say, 'Nah, I don't wanna take him.'

As a youngster, Sterling's footballing talent was prodigious and helped him sign with QPR at the age of 10

Five years later and Sterling had parlayed this into a move to Liverpool's academy, with the star breaking through to the first team in 2012

'At the time, I didn't understand how much she was sacrificing. Her and my mum got me here. My whole family played a massive part in my life. Without them, you wouldn't even know me.'

Football was a necessary focus as well as passion, with Sterling once removed from mainstream education as a youngster and sent to Vernon House, an adapted school to help with behavioral problems.

His teacher there, Chris Beschi, told the Guardian in 2018 that he had said to a young Sterling: 'If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or you'll be in prison.'

But Beschi was able to see a different side to Sterling too, describing the boy as having 'a kind and innocent passion about him', and as football took over, Premier League rivals clamoured to sign him up to their youth ranks.

Nadine was adamant that he should be developed outside of London to avoid any possibility of getting caught up in gang violence, and Chelsea and Arsenal's loss was Liverpool's gain, with Sterling joining the academy at the age of 15 for a then punchy fee of £500,000.

After that, Sterling's career quickly gathered momentum. With the arrival of Liverpool legend Kenny Dalglish in the dugout in early 2011, Sterling was moved into the Europa League squad, fast-tracking integration with established first-team stars. Playing and travel time was limited, however.

Just over a year later, and the player was readied for his first senior start against Wigan Athletic, at the tender age of 17 years and 107 days. The following season saw him named as the club's Young Player of the Year and shortlisted for the PFA Young Player of the Year. By 2014, he was winning the Golden Boy award, and becoming the most expensive English footballer to date with his £49million move to Man City.

But against the backdrop of success on the football pitch, there were challenging moments away from it. In 2013, Sterling was accused of two separate counts of assault, one against a former girlfriend and another against a different woman. He was found not guilty of the former, with the latter incident dropped after a witness failed to attend court.

Two years later, in March 2015, Sterling was snapped by tabloids reportedly smoking from a shisha pipe. And, in a moment that spoke of what was to come, it was alleged that he might have also been using nitrous oxide for recreational purposes. Manager Brendan Rodgers was keen to protect Sterling and urged people to remember: 'Young players make mistakes.'

Sterling had an uneven stint at Liverpool but put on display enough of his talent to earn him the 2014 Golden Boy award

His spell on Merseyside also secured him entrance into the England squad, where he became one of the standouts of the 2010s

Shortly before his move to Man City Sterling started dating Paige Milian, now his long-term partner and mother of his children (Source: Instagram/Raheem Sterling)

The clean slate offered by Man City might have itself been appealing. Things had become somewhat tricky at Anfield, after Sterling had refused a new deal, with the player booed while on duty for England under then-manager Roy Hodgson. Rodgers and Sterling rowed publicly in the media over suggestions that he had turned down a new contract for financial reasons, and his move to the Etihad came after club legends including Steven Gerrard, Jamie Carragher and Graeme Souness had all criticised his conduct.

The first season at the Etihad might have been a false start, with Sterling notably injured in March leading to the premature curtailing of his campaign, but under incoming manager Pep Guardiola, Sterling began flying. At the same time, he was underscoring his importance for England under Hodgson, and then Gareth Southgate.

'In terms of, "Can he fulfil it?", he'll give himself every chance,' Southgate said when asked if he thought Sterling might win the Ballon d'Or after victory against Kosovo in 2019. 'There are some outstanding players around - (Eden) Hazard, (Kevin) De Bruyne, Messi, Ronaldo.

'But he (Sterling) has got the drive, he's got the professionalism, he's got the ability. He's physically and mentally strong for such a small-statured lad.'

And against the backdrop of his growth on the pitch, Sterling was becoming an important voice away from it too, frequently speaking out against the racism young black players were targeted with, and from personal experience. In 2017, Sterling was attacked outside Man City's training ground by a convicted football hooligan hurling racist language at him. In 2018, he suffered racist abuse on the pitch while featuring for Man City against Chelsea.

396 Premier League appearances, 123 goals

GQ magazine described Sterling as football's 'most influential player' in 2019 in recognition of his climb to the very top of the game, and for his increasingly high profile as a campaigner off the pitch.

Sterling branded negative tabloid coverage as racist, and made an address to the United Nations.

'Discrimination is discrimination. It doesn't matter if it's your sexuality, or your color, you shouldn't (discriminate) at all', Sterling said, speaking to the UN Human Rights Office for the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. 'We need – as a collective – to take responsibility. This is a new age where color can't define who you are'.

Sterling also established the Raheem Sterling Foundation in 2021, which the footballer funds and which helps to support youth education projects, including fighting knife crime and helping children out of poverty. That year, he was awarded an MBE for services to racial equality in sport.

As his public profile hit new heights, Sterling kept scoring, becoming Man City's seventh-highest goalscorer of all time. But limited game time under Guardiola led to a move to Chelsea for £47.5m, and on a salary worth an eye-watering £325,000 per week.

Sterling was a focal point of the Man City team which achieved a staggering trophy haul in the late 2010s

His move to Chelsea in 2022 set him up to be one of the stars of the club's new era under BlueCo but he failed to hit the right notes across two personally underwhelming seasons

After an abortive loan move to Arsenal, Sterling signed for Feyenoord at the start of the year but did not see his deal extended past the end of the season

In what might be seen as the beginning of the end, his first season in Chelsea blue failed to hit the heights required. There was chaos in west London as the club cycled through Thomas Tuchel, Graham Potter, Bruno Saltor and Frank Lampard in the dugout but Sterling still bagged nine goals and a further four assists in his 38 appearances, as well as securing a place in Southgate's World Cup squad that year.

Sterling made an impact in the group stages in Qatar, but was forced home after his family home was burgled. While his long-term partner Paige Milian and three children were not at the property, Sterling was shaken and flew back to Oxshott from the camp before returning in time for the quarter-final against France.

While his first season with Chelsea had room for improvement at Stamford Bridge, his second was even limper. The latest manager on the club's merry-go-round, Enzo Maresca, said in August 2024 that he was going to 'struggle' for minutes, effectively frozen out.

From there, his on-pitch decline was swift. An abortive loan across the city to Arsenal had the promise of a step up, but Sterling struggled just as hard for game time. A difficult time was compounded by a second break-in at his home, with the family forced to escape but luckily unharmed.

On his return to Chelsea, Maresca placed him in the now-infamous bomb squad, forced to train away from the first-team players, share separate, smaller locker rooms, and all but ostracised within Cobham.

Offers swirled around Sterling as they have done for all his decorated career, but the possibility of a move to Bayer Leverkusen or Juventus did not go much further than exploratory talks. A switch to nearby Fulham fell through. With money far from a motivating factor, the winger opted not to accept a lucrative contract and move to Saudi Arabia.

Instead, Sterling stayed out of the game until his contract was mutually terminated in January of this year.

Hopes of finding that at his next club Feyenoord evaporated on his debut. Signed until the end of the 2025-26 season, Sterling stepped onto the pitch in February after nine months out and looked rusty.

The critics were brutal, but head coach Robin van Persie did his best to defend his new player. It was too harsh to judge him over just six or eight weeks, he stressed.

Within weeks, he was back in the UK, with his arrest coming in May. Any offers that might have come his way over the summer have subsequently dried up.

Sterling crashed his £270,000 Lambourghini Urus while driving under the influence

The arrest took place shortly after his time in Rotterdam came to an end, with the star pleading guilty in September

Since the arrest, Sterling has been keeping a low profile and focusing on his family (Source: Instagram/Raheem Sterling)

With offers from football clubs quieter, the winger has focused on other ventures including his Playmaker Films (Source: Instagram/Raheem Sterling)

Sterling has since worked on his Playmaker Films, a content agency, and launched 'The Cage', a grassroots football competition where teams of four face off for eight minutes with £5,000 on the line.

'Football's about expressing yourself,' he said when interviewed about why he created the contest, which showcases individuality on caged pitches similar to ones he would have learned to play on. 'The game is a beautiful thing'.

Sterling's story is of a remarkable rise from adversity to the highest levels in professional sport. His private life has clearly been complicated - District Judge Kirsty Allman revealed his drug problem had 'become a maladaptive coping mechanism during a difficult period in his career'.

#1240. Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation

To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Cancer-associated mutations in PIK3CA underlie congenital overgrowth disorders that frequently involve the vasculature1,2. Among the affected tissues, the endothelium commonly exhibits aberrant expansion, leading to vascular malformations3. Notably, these lesions arise predominantly in veins and capillaries, whereas arteries are largely spared, for reasons that remain unclear. Here, using genetic lineage tracing, we show that endothelial expression of PIK3CAH1047R drives profound clonal expansion of capillary and venous endothelial cells, whereas mature arterial endothelial cells are refractory to pathological PI3K activation. Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features, providing a mechanistic explanation for the paucity of arterial lesions after PIK3CA genetic perturbation. Mechanistically, these effects are mediated by two complementary downstream branches of PI3K signalling: increased proliferation, which drives vascular overgrowth, and upregulation of the venous-specifying transcription factor NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), which suppresses arterial differentiation. Together, our findings reveal that pathogenic responses to PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial differentiation state and fate trajectory, and demonstrate that arterial endothelium is intrinsically resistant to oncogenic PI3K signalling. Arteries are therefore shielded from PIK3CA mutations, explaining the rarity of arterial malformations in PIK3CA-driven disease.

Somatic and germline pathogenic variants in cancer-associated genes cause diverse congenital disorders1,2 and are also found in phenotypically normal tissue4,5. Germline mutations may be inherited or arise de novo, whereas somatic mutations, acquired during embryonic development, generate mosaicism and a broad spectrum of phenotypes1. Understanding how identical mutations produce distinct outcomes across tissues is crucial for defining cellular susceptibility to disease and explaining the phenotypic heterogeneity.

PIK3CA encodes p110α, the catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3Kα), which regulates cell growth, proliferation, migration and metabolism6 through AKT and downstream effectors, including mTOR and forkhead box O (FOXO) transcription factors7,8. PIK3CA is an oncogene that is frequently mutated in both mosaic congenital disorders9 and phenotypically normal tissue4. Activating mutations occur throughout the coding sequence, with recurrent hotspots including E545K, E542K, H1047R and H1047L3. Mesoderm-derived tissues, including the endothelium, are commonly affected in PIK3CA-related congenital disorders, which manifest as aberrant tissue overgrowth and vascular malformations10,11,12,13. Although PIK3CA mutations have been extensively studied in adult epithelial tissues14,15,16,17, their effects on cellular heterogeneity, differentiation and clonal dynamics in mesoderm-derived lineages remain poorly understood.

Vascular malformations are congenital vascular anomalies classified as slow-flow lesions, affecting capillaries, veins and lymphatic vessels or fast-flow lesions, often involving arteries18. Somatic activating PIK3CA mutations occur in the endothelium of all major slow-flow vascular malformations, where lesion expansion requires mitogenic signals, even though the mutation alone is insufficient to confer a proliferative advantage19,20,21,22. By contrast, no evidence currently implicates PIK3CA mutations in fast-flow arterial malformations3. Whether arterial endothelial cells have these mutations but resist their effects, or mutant clones are negatively selected or eliminated in arterial vessels remains unclear.

Here we demonstrate that endothelial responses to oncogenic PIK3CAH1047R are governed by cellular identity and developmental trajectory. Combining mosaic genetics, lineage tracing and single-cell analyses, we identify a differentiation-stage-specific window of susceptibility to pathological PI3K signalling, while fully differentiated arterial endothelial cells are resistant. These findings provide a framework for the tissue and vessel-type specificity of PIK3CA-driven vascular malformations.

Postnatal expression of Pik3caH1047R (Pik3catm1.1Waph/+) from the endogenous locus in mouse retinal endothelial cells using Pdgfb-creERT2 results in venous and capillary malformations, whereas arteries remain unaffected19 (Extended Data Fig. 1a–e). To correlate these phenotypes with the distribution of mutant cells, we introduced the R26-mTmG reporter allele into the Pik3caH1047RPdgfb-creERT2 mice (pan-endothelial (pEC)-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 1a). Tamoxifen-mediated Cre activation induced recombination of the endogenous Pik3caH1047R allele and the reporter, resulting in membrane-bound GFP expression that marks recombined cells and therefore approximates Pik3caH1047R-expressing endothelial cells. Pdgfb-creERT2R26-mTmG mice were used as controls (pEC-GFP). After low-dose administration of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at postnatal day 1 (P1), retinas were analysed at P6 (Extended Data Fig. 1c). Mosaic recombination was observed throughout the vascular plexus in both genotypes (Fig. 1b). Although GFP+ mutant cells were present in all vessel types, vascular malformations occurred exclusively in capillaries and veins (Fig. 1c,d). In these vessels, mutant GFP+ endothelial cells underwent marked clonal expansion, generating enlarged vascular tubes (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1f), accompanied by increased endothelial cell proliferation during early lesion formation (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i). By contrast, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells in arteries neither expanded nor altered vessel width (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 1f). Consistent with these phenotypes, capillary and venous mutant GFP+ cells displayed increased PI3K pathway activation, as assessed by staining of phosphorylated S6 (p-S6), whereas arterial mutant cells showed no detectable increase relative to wild-type (WT) cells (Fig. 1d,f). These data show that Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells selectively expand in capillaries and veins, while arteries remain structurally and molecularly normal despite containing mutant cells.

a, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and endothelial populations targeted by low-dose 4-OHT-induced Pdgfb-creERT2 activation; pEC, pan-endothelial cells. b, Confocal images of P6 retinas stained for IB4 (red, blood vessels) and GFP (cyan/grey, Pdgfb-targeted endothelial cells). c, The incidence of vascular malformations in P6 pEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas (n = 8 retinas). d, High-magnification confocal images of P6 retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and p-S6 (Ser235/236) (yellow/grey, PI3K readout). The white dotted rectangles indicate the regions magnified on the right. e,f, Quantification of GFP+ area (n = 13, 19, 5, 15, 5 and 13 retinas, left to right) (e) and p-S6 fluorescence within GFP+ areas (n = 6, 8, 5, 8, 5 and 7 retinas, left to right) (f) in capillaries, veins and arteries. g, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and endothelial population targeted by 4-OHT-induced Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 activation. aEC, arterial endothelial cells. h,i, Confocal images of P9 aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (red) and GFP (cyan, Bmx-targeted endothelial cells) (h) or IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and p-S6 (grey) (i). j,k, GFP+ arterial area (n = 6 and 11 retinas, left to right) (j) and p-S6 fluorescence within GFP+ areas (n = 6 and 7 retinas, left to right) (k). Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (e,f,j,k). Scale bars, 150 μm (b,h) and 30 μm (d,i). FC, fold change; NS, not significant.

The apparent resistance of arterial endothelial cells to Pik3caH1047R prompted us to directly investigate the behaviour of mutant cells in arteries. To this end, we used the Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 mouse line, which specifically targets arterial endothelial cells in retinal vessels. WT and Pik3caH1047R arterial endothelial cells (aEC) were traced by combining Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 and R26-mTmG with or without the Pik3caH1047R allele (aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 1g). Bmx(PAC)-creERT2-mediated tracing revealed robust arterial recombination after 4-OHT administration at P4 or P7, whereas induction at P1 did not label arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). Thus, recombination was induced at P4 or P7 for subsequent experiments. In both settings, the proportion of GFP+ cells and arterial vessel width were comparable between the mutant and control retinas (Fig. 1h–j and Extended Data Fig. 2c–f). Arteries also displayed similar smooth-muscle-cell coverage and maintained expression of arterial markers UNC5B and CX37 (Extended Data Fig. 2g–j). Moreover, GFP+ arterial endothelial cells of both genotypes lacked expression of NR2F2, a key transcription factor that suppresses arterial identity23,24,25,26 (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). Consistent with earlier observations, mutant GFP+ cells showed low PI3K pathway activation, with no increase relative to controls (Fig. 1i,k and Extended Data Fig. 2m,n). To assess the long-term effects, we analysed retinas at P21. No differences were detected in the GFP+ cell distribution, arterial morphology or NR2F2 expression between WT and Pik3caH1047R cells in main arteries and arteriolar branches (Extended Data Fig. 2o–q). These findings show that mutant cells persist in arteries or arteriolar branches without detectable changes in arterial identity, morphology or PI3K activation, supporting the resistance of differentiated arterial endothelial cells to Pik3caH1047R.

To investigate why arterial endothelial cells are protected against Pik3caH1047R, we pharmacologically disrupted key arterial features in aEC-GFP and aEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R pups. As arterial endothelial cells experience higher shear stress, we first reduced systemic blood pressure with the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor captopril27. Although captopril reduced KLF4 expression and induced dilation of the vascular plexus28, it did not alter the proportion of GFP+ cells or arterial width. Furthermore, endothelial proliferation was not increased in mutant arteries (Extended Data Fig. 3a–d). We next inhibited Notch signalling, a key regulator of arterial differentiation and maintenance, using N-[N-(3,5-difluorophenacetyl)-l-alanyl]-S-phenylglycine t-butyl ester (DAPT). Despite a pronounced response in sprouting capillaries, DAPT likewise did not elicit any response in arteries to Pik3caH1047R expression (Extended Data Fig. 3a,e,f). Collectively, these results indicate that inhibition of major arterial identity programmes alone is insufficient to overcome arterial resistance to Pik3caH1047R.

To test whether resistance to Pik3caH1047R emerges during arterial differentiation, we traced tip endothelial cells—a pre-arterial population that contributes to arterial growth29,30. We used the Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 mouse line, which specifically marks tip cells, crossed with R26-mTmG (tEC-GFP) alone or in combination with Pik3caH1047R (tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R; Fig. 2a). 4-OHT was administered at P1, and Esm1-GFP+ progeny were analysed at different timepoints (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Then, 24 h after induction, GFP+ cells were predominantly localized at the sprouting front (Fig. 2b). By P6, GFP+ cells contributed extensively to arteries in tEC-GFP retinas, and the GFP+ arterial area further increased by P8 (Fig. 2b). Consistent with previous reports30, a subset of Esm1-traced cells also contributed to the capillary plexus (Fig. 2b). Pik3caH1047R expression markedly reduced the GFP+ area within arteries (Fig. 2b–f and Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). Instead, most mutant GFP+ cells were retained in the capillary bed, where they expanded (Fig. 2d,f and Extended Data Fig. 4b–f) and formed multiple vascular malformations (Fig. 2b,c). Moreover, mutant, but not control, GFP+ cells were frequently detected in veins (Fig. 2b–f and Extended Data Fig. 4b,c). The few Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells that reached arteries did not induce pathology (Fig. 2c). Consistent with lesion formation, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells displayed increased p-S6 levels in capillaries, but not in arteries (Fig. 2e,g and Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). By P21, Pik3caH1047R GFP+ clones persisted in capillaries and veins, although they did not further expand (Extended Data Fig. 4i–l). These data indicate that Pik3caH1047R expression impairs mobilization of arterial precursors to arteries, resulting in their retention within capillaries and the diversion of a subset towards veins, where they expand and form vascular malformations.

Yellow and blue nuclei indicate mutant and WT cells, respectively. i, Confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas stained for IB4 (magenta), Cherry (cyan, WT) and eGFP (yellow, PIK3CAH1047R-expressing cells). A, artery; V, vein. The cyan arrows indicate WT cells. Representative of 30 retinas across 10 independent experiments. j, The distribution of recombined Cherry+ and eGFP+ Esm1-derived progeny within arteries and capillaries/veins at P8. The numbers indicate cell counts and percentages. n = 6 retinas. k, High-magnification confocal images of P8 tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R retinas. The arrow indicates an arterial lesion. l,m, The percentage of Ki-67+ cells (n = 6 retinas) (l) and p-S6 fluorescence (n = 4 retinas) (m) in Cherry+ and eGFP+ capillary endothelial cells. n, Arteries containing Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells among arteries containing recombined endothelial cells (n = 14 retinas). Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (f,g,l,m). Scale bars, 150 μm (b,i) and 30 μm (d,e,k).

To directly compare WT and mutant endothelial cells within the same tissue, we generated a multispectral genetic mouse model, termed iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R (Rosa26CAG-LSL-H2B-Cherry/H2B-GFP-2A-HAHuPIK3CAH1047R). Cre-mediated recombination stochastically generates either His-H2B-Cherry (WT) or H2B-eGFP-V5 together with HA-PIK3CAH1047R (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Validation in primary endothelial cells confirmed preferential generation of Cherry+ cells, as reported for related constructs31, and increased proliferation and PI3K pathway activation in eGFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5b–h). To fate-map pre-arterial endothelial cells in vivo, we crossed iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R mice with Esm1(BAC)-creERT2 mice (tEC-iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R) (Fig. 2h). As the recombination efficiency was lower than in Pik3catm1.1Waph/+ mice, we increased the 4-OHT dose, and retinas were analysed 7 days after induction (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Cherry+ cells contributed to both capillaries and arteries (Fig. 2i–k). By contrast, eGFP+ cells were predominantly located in capillaries, including those adjacent to arteries, and in veins, where they expanded and formed vascular malformations (Fig. 2i–k and Extended Data Fig. 6b). eGFP+ cells greatly outnumbered Cherry+ cells (7,680 versus 511) and displayed increased Ki-67 positivity and p-S6 levels (Fig. 2j,l,m and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Despite their expansion, only 0.47% of total eGFP+ cells was incorporated into arteries, compared with 23% of Cherry+ cells (Fig. 2j). Overall, mutant endothelial cells were detected in only 16% of arteries containing recombined cells (Fig. 2n). Co-staining for eGFP, Cherry and ERG confirmed that lesions consisted exclusively of mutant cells (Extended Data Fig. 6e).

In contrast to Esm1+ cells expressing Pik3caH1047R from the endogenous locus, which did not induce arterial pathology (Fig. 2c,e), all eGFP+ cells that reached arteries in the iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R model formed small lesions (averaging nine cells per lesion) (Fig. 2k). We therefore tested whether forced overexpression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial endothelial cells would produce a similar phenotype. To this end, we combined iFluMosaic-PIK3CAH1047R with Bmx(PAC)-creERT2 and induced recombination between P4 and P6, or between P7 and P9 (Extended Data Fig. 6f–i). Five days later, the expected proportions of Cherry+ and eGFP+ cells were detected (Extended Data Fig. 6h). Mutant arterial cells remained non-pathogenic after late recombination; however, targeting at P4–6 resulted in mild arterial overgrowth in around 20% of arteries containing recombined mutant cells (Extended Data Fig. 6f–i). Across models, arterial width inversely correlated with endothelial differentiation state at the time of PIK3CAH1047R expression (Extended Data Fig. 6i). eGFP+ arterial endothelial cells showed increased PI3K signalling activation compared with neighbouring Cherry+ cells under all conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6g,j). By contrast, endogenous Pik3caH1047R expression did not increase arterial p-S6 levels (Figs. 1d,f,i,k and 2e,g). Nonetheless, eGFP+ arterial cells still lacked NR2F2 expression (Extended Data Fig. 6k), consistent with maintained arterial identity. Together, these data indicate that arterial resistance to PIK3CAH1047R depends on endothelial differentiation state and mutant expression level. Forced overexpression partially overcomes this resistance at earlier developmental stages, promoting mild arterial overgrowth without inducing NR2F2 expression.

To investigate how Pik3caH1047R impairs arterial mobilization, we analysed endothelial cell transcriptomes using single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. We profiled endothelial cells from tEC-GFP (6,564 cells) and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R (19,168 cells) retinas, enabling molecular tracing of Esm1+ tip cells and their progeny (Fig. 3a). We first defined endothelial transcriptional states in WT retinas by clustering scRNA-seq data from tEC-GFP retinas. Unsupervised analysis identified nine populations: tip, pre-arterial angiogenic, metabolic angiogenic, proliferative 1, proliferative 2, venous, capillary, arterial capillary and arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7a–c and Supplementary Data 1). Notably, hierarchical clustering based on average gene expression profiles grouped tip, proliferative and metabolic angiogenic populations together, whereas pre-arterial angiogenic endothelial cells were more similar to arterial and arterial-capillary populations, supporting their arterial bias (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Traced cells were identified by GFP transcripts (Extended Data Fig. 7e). Projection of GFP expression onto the uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) revealed Esm1-traced cells in all clusters except for the venous population (Extended Data Fig. 7f–h). Approximately half of Esm1-traced cells localized to arterial populations, whereas around 20% remained proliferative, indicating that Esm1-derived endothelial cells normally retain proliferative capacity while progressively differentiating into the arterial lineage (Extended Data Fig. 7h).

a, Schematic of the transgenic strategy and the experimental timeline. b, UMAP of merged P6 tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinal endothelial cells derived from scRNA-seq. aCap, arterial capillary endothelial cells; vEC, venous endothelial cells. c, Selected cluster marker genes. The dot size and colour indicate the frequency and expression level, respectively. d, UMAP of GFP+ endothelial cells (Esm1-derived progeny) from tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas. e, The distribution of GFP+ endothelial cells across clusters. f, Differential gene expression between GFP+ mutant and WT endothelial cells across clusters, highlighting arterial, tip/pre-arterial and venous-associated signatures. The dot colour indicates the log2-transformed FC value and the size indicates significance (adjusted P < 0.05). g, Confocal images of P6 sprouting fronts stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan) and UNC5B (yellow). The white and orange arrows indicate GFP+UNC5Bhigh and GFP+UNC5Blow endothelial cells, respectively. h, Confocal images of P6 capillaries stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan), ERG (blue) and NR2F2 (yellow). The white and red arrows indicate ERG+NR2F2− and ERG+NR2F2+ cells within the GFP+ area, respectively. i, UNC5B fluorescence in GFP+ cells at the sprouting front (n = 4 retinas). j, The percentage of NR2F2+ERG+ nuclei relative to total ERG+ nuclei within GFP+ capillary areas (n = 6 and 5 retinas, left to right). The colours indicate the proportions of NR2F2high and NR2F2low cells within the NR2F2+ population. k,l, Confocal images of P4 (k) and P6 (l) retinas stained for IB4 (red), GFP (cyan), ERG (blue) and EdU (yellow). The red arrows indicate EdU+ERG+ cells within GFP+ areas. m, EdU+ERG+ cells relative to total ERG+ cells within GFP+ areas (n = 4 retinas). Data are mean ± s.e.m. Statistical analysis was performed using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (i and j) and two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Šidák’s multiple-comparison test (m). Scale bars, 60 μm (g) and 20 μm (h,k,l).

We next examined whether Pik3caH1047R affects this developmental trajectory. To address this, we jointly analysed WT and Pik3caH1047R endothelial cells. Integrated analysis resolved seven endothelial populations: tip (C1), metabolic angiogenic (C2), proliferative 1 (C3), proliferative 2 (C4), venous (C5), arterial capillary (C6) and arterial (C7) endothelial cells (Fig. 3b,c, Extended Data Fig. 7i and Supplementary Data 1). GFP expression revealed a marked redistribution of Esm1-traced cells (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7j,k). Whereas WT GFP+ cells predominantly localized to arterial capillary and arterial clusters (C6 and C7), Pik3caH1047R GFP+ cells were instead enriched within angiogenic, proliferative and venous clusters (C2, C3, C4 and C5) (Fig. 3d,e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Quantification confirmed selective expansion of mutant GFP+ cells in proliferative, angiogenic and venous clusters, but not arterial clusters (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 7k). Importantly, Pik3ca expression was comparable across all endothelial clusters (Extended Data Fig. 7l).

To determine whether this redistribution also reflected altered endothelial transcriptional identity, we performed cluster-specific differential expression analysis comparing GFP+ WT and GFP+ Pik3caH1047R endothelial populations. We identified transcriptional alterations between WT and mutant cells in all clusters, with only limited changes in arterial cells (C7), consistent with the resistance observed in differentiated arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7m). The tip cluster (C1) contained too few cells for robust differential expression analysis (Extended Data Fig. 7k). Affected clusters showed a consistent shift towards venous-associated gene expression, accompanied by reduced tip, arterial, guidance and capillary-specialization programmes (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 7n). This pattern remained after correcting for differences in cluster size (Supplementary Fig. 1). Hierarchical clustering further showed the greatest genotype-dependent divergence in angiogenic and venous populations (Extended Data Fig. 7o). We next performed RNA velocity analysis on subclustered GFP+ cells, which revealed altered cell-state dynamics in Esm1-traced mutant endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 7p,q and Supplementary Data 1). Whereas WT GFP+ cells displayed coherent trajectories toward capillary and arterial states, mutant cells showed altered cell-state trajectories, with prominent progression toward proliferative and venous-associated populations and reduced progression toward the arterial lineage (Extended Data Fig. 7r). Together, these findings indicate that Pik3caH1047R promotes endothelial proliferation while diverting differentiating endothelial cells away from the arterial programme towards venous-associated cell states.

To determine whether this programme is initiated rapidly after Pik3caH1047R expression, we analysed cultured sister endothelial cells derived from Pik3caH1047RPdgfb-creERT2 mice using scRNA-seq (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b and Supplementary Data 2). Endothelial identity across clusters was confirmed by uniform Pecam1 expression, and Pik3ca expression was comparable between clusters (Extended Data Fig. 8c,d). Acute Pik3caH1047R expression recapitulated the in vivo transcriptional changes, with expansion of proliferative and venous-like populations and reduction of tip/arterial endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 8e–g). Mutant cells also expressed higher levels of venous markers (that is, Nr2f2 and Nrp2) and lower levels of tip markers (that is, Esm1 and Angpt2) (Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). These data indicate that Pik3caH1047R rapidly and cell-autonomously initiates a programme of proliferation and loss of arterial identity.

We next examined how this transcriptional transition unfolds during arterial differentiation in vivo by staining tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas at P4 and P6 for UNC5B and NR2F2. Control GFP+ cells expressed UNC5B by P4 while remaining NR2F2 negative at both timepoints (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–l). Mutant GFP+ cells were similar to controls at P4 but, by P6, showed reduced UNC5B expression at the sprouting front and near arteries, along with ectopic NR2F2 expression (Fig. 3g–j and Extended Data Fig. 8j–n). These findings validate the scRNA-seq data and demonstrate that Pik3caH1047R progressively disrupts arterial differentiation in vivo.

To establish the temporal relationship between hyperproliferation and arterial differentiation defects, we examined the proliferative behaviour of Esm1-traced cells at P4 and P6. EdU incorporation showed that Esm1-traced cells normally retain proliferative capacity at P4, with proliferation beginning to diminish by P6 (Fig. 3k–m). Pik3caH1047R mutant Esm1-traced cells exhibited the same temporal pattern, although proliferation remained markedly higher at both timepoints, indicating that hyperproliferation precedes ectopic NR2F2 induction (Fig. 3k–m). The absence of a further increase in proliferation after NR2F2 induction at P6 argues against NR2F2 driving endothelial hyperproliferation.

To test whether hyperproliferation accounts for defective arterial differentiation, we treated tEC-GFP and tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R mice with the CDK4 and CDK6 inhibitor palbociclib. Palbociclib partially reduced endothelial proliferation and vascular hyperplasia in tEC-GFP-Pik3caH1047R retinas but did not restore arterial differentiation or suppress NR2F2 expression (Fig. 4a–h). Similar results were obtained with mitomycin C, which robustly inhibited endothelial expansion without restoring arterial incorporation or reducing NR2F2 expression in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 9a–i). Consistently, palbociclib inhibited cell cycle progression in vitro but did not prevent Pik3caH1047R-driven NR2F2 upregulation (Fig. 4i–k and Extended Data Fig. 9j–m). Together, these findings show that suppressing proliferation does not prevent NR2F2 induction or restore arterial differentiation, supporting distinct effects of Pik3caH1047R signalling on proliferation and arterial specification. Consistent with this interpretation, scRNA-seq analysis revealed no association between Nr2f2 expression and cell cycle status in mutant GFP+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 10a).
